title: Inflation and your money
desc: Real return, CPI and why hot inflation keeps rates higher

cards.title: Richer or poorer?
cards.situation: Your savings earned 3% this year. Prices in the shops rose 5%. Did you get richer?

options.feedback: You have more dollars, but each one buys less. Prices rose faster than your savings.

options.text: No: you can buy about 2% less
options.feedback: More dollars, less stuff. Your real return was about −2%.
It doesn’t even out: prices rose 5% and your savings only 3%. You can buy about 2% less.

cards.work: $10,000 grew to $10,300. Goods that cost $10,000 now cost $10,500. Real return ≈ 3% − 5% = −2%.

cards.title: Inflation: prices going up
cards.text: **[[inflation|Inflation]]** is how fast prices rise. Most countries track it with the **[[cpi|CPI]]**: the cost of a basket of everyday goods.

blocks.tip: **[[real-return|Real return]]** = your return − inflation. It’s what your money can actually buy.

cards.title: Why central banks raise rates
cards.text: Most central banks aim for inflation near 2%. When it runs hot, they use rates to cool it.

items.title: Loans cost more, so people and firms spend less

cards.foot: A hot inflation report can mean more hikes. That’s why markets watch CPI so closely.

cards.title: Is cash always safe?
cards.myth: Money in the bank is safe from inflation.
cards.reality: Cash keeps its number, not its buying power. At 3% inflation, $10,000 kept in cash for 10 years buys only what about $7,400 buys today.

cards.title: Find the real return
cards.q: You hold a bond paying 6% a year. Inflation is 4%. What is your real return?

visual.title: This year
visual.label: Bond pays 6%, inflation is 4%, real return unknown

options.feedback: Inflation is taken away, not added. Real return is what’s left after prices rise.
6% is what the bond pays before inflation. Take inflation away to find what you really earn.
The bond pays 6% and prices rise 4%, so your buying power grows about 2% a year.
That takes away the wrong way round. The bond pays more than inflation, so the real return is positive.

cards.title: Hotter than expected
cards.q: Markets expected inflation of 3%. The CPI report shows 4%. What might traders now expect from the central bank?

options.feedback: Hot inflation is a reason to keep rates high, not to cut them.
Hot inflation gives the central bank a reason to keep rates high, so traders push back their hopes of cuts.
One hot report doesn’t make prices fall. It shows they’re still rising fast.
CPI is one of the main numbers central banks watch when they set rates.

cards.headline: You can see past the headline number.
lines: Inflation is how fast prices rise, tracked by CPI.
Hot inflation often means higher rates for longer.
